questions.question: What is the done-channel pattern in Go?
questions.title: Done Channel Pattern
questions.direct_answer: A chan struct{} that signals 'stop' by CLOSING. Workers select on <-done; close(done) wakes ALL simultaneously. close is the broadcast; receiving the zero value IS the message.

sections.title: Quick Revision
sections.content: A chan struct{} that signals 'stop' by CLOSING. Workers select on <-done; close(done) wakes ALL simultaneously. close is the broadcast; receiving the zero value IS the message.

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
The pattern:

```go
done := make(chan struct{})
results := make(chan int, 5)
go func() {
    for i := 0; i < 5; i++ {
        select {
        case <-done:          // stop signal
            close(results)
            return
        case results <- i:    // do work
        }
    }
    close(results)
}()

close(done)   // ALL workers selecting on done wake immediately
for v := range results { fmt.Print(v, " ") }  // 0 1 2 3 4 — executed
```

Why CLOSE (not a value): a send wakes ONE receiver; a close wakes EVERY receiver — the broadcast. And close is permanent: every receive after returns immediately. The TYPE — chan struct{} — signals 'zero bytes of payload; the channel exists for its close.'

The combination: done + results, each closed by its owner — the lifecycle is explicit and every receiver terminates cleanly.

What context.Context generalizes: ctx.Done() IS this channel (a <-chan struct{}), and ctx.Cancel() is close. The bare done-channel is the mechanism to learn first; context adds deadlines, values, and parent-child trees on top.

sections.title: Mental Model
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart TD
    CLOSE[close done] --> B[broadcast — wakes ALL receivers]
    W1[worker 1] -.->|sees close| R1[return]
    W2[worker 2] -.->|sees close| R2[return]
    B --> W1
    B --> W2
```

sections.title: Deep Dive
sections.content:
The broadcast mechanics: close(ch) sets the closed flag and wakes every parked receiver. Each returns (zero, false) — forever. This is WHY close is the cancellation primitive: a send could wake one; a close can't be missed by any goroutine selecting now or later.

The struct{} payload: the done channel carries NO data — the message IS the closure. struct{} costs zero bytes. chan bool works but communicates 'a boolean will be sent.' struct{} says 'there is no message.'

The worker-loop shape: for { select { case <-done: return; case work := <-queue: process(work) } }. The select BEFORE each work item checks done — cancellable between items. The ordering choice (check before vs after) is the semantics: stop-immediately vs stop-after-current (graceful drain).

The context evolution: this pattern WAS the pre-context idiom. ctx.Done() is the done channel; the API adds deadline propagation, values, and the cancellation error (cancelled vs deadline-exceeded). Both are the same mechanism underneath.
